lessons.title: Early humans and the Stone Age

objectives: Describe how the earliest humans lived
Explain the importance of tools and fire
Distinguish the Old and New Stone Age
Explain why Africa is important for the story of humankind
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify the terms and approximate time ranges; this lesson gives no numerical dates for human origins on purpose.

blocks.md: The earliest humans lived a very long time ago, many hundreds of thousands of years before writing. Fossils and tools found by archaeologists show that humans began to develop in **Africa**, especially in East and Southern Africa, and later spread to other continents. For this reason Africa is often called the **cradle of humankind**.

blocks.caption: Steps in the Stone Age
blocks.alt: Four boxes from hunting and gathering to the beginning of farming.

blocks.title: Old Stone Age
blocks.md: In the **Old Stone Age** (Palaeolithic) people were **hunter-gatherers**: they hunted animals, fished and gathered fruits, roots and honey. They moved from place to place following food, lived in caves, rock shelters or simple huts, and made tools from **stone**, **bone** and **wood**. They learned to **control fire**.

blocks.title: Why tools and fire mattered
blocks.md: Tools helped people to cut, scrape, hunt and defend themselves. **Fire** gave warmth, light and protection from wild animals, cooked food and hardened wooden tools. People also developed **language**, worked in groups and made **paintings** on rock walls in many parts of the world, including Africa.

Later, in the **New Stone Age** (Neolithic), people made finer polished stone tools, made pottery, and — most importantly — began to **farm**. Groups no longer had to roam all the time. We use the names 'Old' and 'New' for stages of development, not for fixed dates, because they began at different times in different places.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Early humans did not all live in caves: many used open camps and huts.
- 'Stone Age' does not mean people only used stone; they also used wood and bone, which rot and rarely survive.
- Our evidence is incomplete: new discoveries may change what historians say.

blocks.title: Example 1: how did they live?
blocks.statement: Describe how a group of Old Stone Age people got their food.
steps: They hunted and fished and collected wild fruits, roots and honey.
They moved when food became scarce.
blocks.answer: By hunting, fishing and gathering wild foods, moving as needed.

blocks.title: Example 2: uses of fire
blocks.statement: Give two ways in which the use of fire helped early people.
steps: It protected them from animals and allowed cooking.
Cooked food is easier to eat and safer.

lessons.title: The farming revolution and the use of iron
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 1 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain how farming began and its effects
Explain the importance of iron working in Africa
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify the approximate date of the first farmers and the spread of ironworking in Africa (kept as 'about 10 000 years' and 'more than two thousand years ago').

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: Some 10 000 years ago, in several parts of the world, people learned to **plant crops** and **keep animals**. This change is called the **farming (agricultural) revolution**. It happened in different places at different times. In Africa, people domesticated crops such as sorghum, millet and yams and kept cattle, goats and sheep.

blocks.caption: A change in way of life
blocks.alt: Two columns comparing hunting and gathering with farming.

blocks.title: Effects of farming
blocks.md: People could **settle** in one place and build **villages**; food became more plentiful and could be **stored**; the population grew; and some people could do other jobs (pottery, weaving, toolmaking, trading) instead of farming: this is **specialisation**. Settlements grew, leaders appeared, and trade between communities developed.

Farming also brought problems: harvests could fail because of drought or pests, settlements could be attacked, and sharing land and water could cause disputes. People developed rules, customs and leaders to settle these problems, and the first **towns** and **states** later grew from such village communities.

blocks.title: The Iron Age
blocks.md: People learned to extract **iron** from ore by heating it in a furnace, then shaped it with **blacksmith** skills. Iron hoes, axes, spears and knives were stronger than stone tools, so people could clear forest, farm more land and hunt and fight better. Iron working spread widely across Africa more than two thousand years ago, and blacksmiths often held a special place in society.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The change to farming was gradual, not a single day; it happened at different times in different places.
- Farming did not mean everybody became wealthier: some groups preferred hunting or herding.
- Iron did not replace stone everywhere at the same time.

blocks.title: Example 1: effects of farming
blocks.statement: Why did farming lead to the growth of villages?
steps: Farmers had to stay near their fields and store the harvest.
So they built permanent homes and villages.
blocks.answer: Farmers had to stay near fields and stores, so villages grew.

blocks.title: Example 2: advantages of iron
blocks.statement: Why was an iron hoe better than a stone hoe?
steps: Iron is harder and less likely to break.
It can be sharpened and shaped.
So work was faster and more land could be cleared.
blocks.answer: It is stronger, can be sharpened and clears more land.
